titleStmt.title: Auditory stimuli elicit hippocampal neuronal responses during sleep
titleStmt.author: Vinnik
Antopolskiy
Itskov
Diamond

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Auditory stimuli elicit hippocampal neuronal responses during sleep

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how hippocampal CA1 neurons respond to sounds that predict reward, and whether they still respond outside the task
span.quote: To investigate how hippocampal neurons code behaviorally salient stimuli, we recorded from neurons in the CA1 region of hippocampus in rats while they learned to associate the presence of sound with water reward.

span.label: whether hippocampal sound responses survive when the animal is not engaged in a discrimination task, including during sleep
span.quote: In the current experiment we characterized responses of hippocampal neurons to behaviorally relevant sounds which were played during sleep and to awake passively listening rats. In the behavioral task, the sounds cued the upcoming release of a reward. Outside the task, the sounds were unrelated to the animal's behavior.

span.label: distinguishes two kinds of hippocampal sound response - a short-latency onset response present even in sleep, and a longer sound-specific response tied to task engagement
span.quote: Based on the current findings and the results of previous experiments we described the existence of two types of hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds: sound-onset responses with very short latency and longer-lasting sound-specific responses that are likely to be present when the animal is actively engaged in the task.

span.label: existence
span.quote: In this study we show that a significant subset of hippocampal neurons responds to sounds presented passively to a rat during both quiet wakefulness and during sleep.

span.label: hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds during sleep
span.quote: In the current experiment we characterized responses of hippocampal neurons to behaviorally relevant sounds which were played during sleep and to awake passively listening rats.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: To investigate how hippocampal neurons code behaviorally salient stimuli, we recorded from neurons in the CA1 region of hippocampus in rats while they learned to associate the presence of sound with water reward.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Thirst plus placement in a completely novel dim environment raises the animal's attention to the sounds, which is why hippocampal neurons responded here although they did not in the earlier over-trained, satiated condition
span.quote: In the present study the animals were thirsty during passive presentation and were placed in a completely novel dim environment, which could have facilitated attention to the auditory stimuli.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Short-latency hippocampal responses are suppressed once the animal comes to expect the stimulus, so over-training or satiation abolishes them
span.quote: These responses are not present in the over-trained and/or satiated animals suggesting that they might disappear when the animal expects the stimuli.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Sound-evoked CA1 responses are driven anatomically by perforant path terminals from entorhinal cortex, or polysynaptically through the Schaffer collaterals
span.quote: The evoked responses in the CA1 region may be generated by perforant path terminals, originating in the entorhinal cortex or polisynaptically via the Schaffer collaterals.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Persistent sustained firing, of the kind described in entorhinal cortex, holds the stimulus trace after stimulus offset and thereby produces the long-lasting responses
span.quote: This memory trace could be stored by sustained activity, previously described in entorhinal cortex (Egorov et al., 2002 ), or by some other cellular or network mechanisms in higher order associative cortices or hippocampus itself.

span.label: the lottery design holds position and motivational state constant between sound and no-sound trials, since both begin with the same nosepoke
span.quote: Trials with and without sound presentation were compared, assuring that the animal was in exactly the same position and motivational state in both types of trials.

span.label: the 50% schedule was introduced specifically to raise reward salience and make the animal attend to the sounds
span.quote: On the fifth day of the training, the reinforcement schedule was changed to increase the salience of the reward and, especially, to make the rat attend to novel sounds associated with reward.

span.label: long randomised inter-stimulus intervals of 25-30 s were used to reduce adaptation to repetition
span.quote: The long inter-stimulus interval was intended to reduce the animal's adaptation to stimulus repetitions

span.label: responses are tested at four a-priori bin sizes and a neuron counts as responsive if any bin survives FDR correction
span.quote: To take into account the variability of the responses (e.g., fast transient or sustained responses), we used four a-priori defined bin sizes (50 ms, 500 ms, 1 and 2 s).

span.label: only sleep trials that produced no visible behavioural response were analysed
span.quote: Only the trials where sounds did not cause any visible behavioral response from the sleeping animal were analyzed further.

span.label: Usable neuronal data came from only two of the six trained animals.
span.quote: Neuronal data suitable for analysis was collected from two animals.

span.label: Too few neurons were recorded to conclude anything about a single neuron's properties across sessions and contexts.
span.quote: Although we were able to keep the same neurons across the recording sessions, as evidenced by the neuronal waveforms, autocorrelations and firing rates, we feel that the number of recorded neurons does not allow us to make any conclusive statements regarding a single neuron's properties across time and context.

span.label: The dataset is too small to draw further conclusions about whether the long-responding cells were putative interneurons.
span.quote: Unfortunately, limited size of our dataset does not allow us to make any further conclusions on this issue.

span.label: usable neuronal data came from two animals, out of six trained and four implanted
span.quote: Out of the six animals trained to perform the behavioral task, four were implanted using microdrives for chronic recordings. Neuronal data suitable for analysis was collected from two animals.

span.label: the authors decline to track single neurons across contexts despite having the waveforms, because the sample is too small
span.quote: Although we were able to keep the same neurons across the recording sessions, as evidenced by the neuronal waveforms, autocorrelations and firing rates, we feel that the number of recorded neurons does not allow us to make any conclusive statements regarding a single neuron's properties across time and context.

span.label: the putative-interneuron identification of the long-response cells is explicitly not pursued for the same reason
span.quote: Both of these neurons are likely to be putative interneurons because of the narrow spike width and the absence of the 3–4 ms peak in the autocorrelation plot (data not shown). Unfortunately, limited size of our dataset does not allow us to make any further conclusions on this issue.

span.label: none of the passively responding neurons distinguished between the sounds
span.quote: None of the three sound-responding neurons discriminated between different sounds i.e., their responses to different sounds were identical.

span.label: six male rats only
span.quote: Six male rats weighing about 350 g were housed individually and maintained on a 14 h/10 h light/dark cycle.

span.label: artificial vowels with formant structure, imported as a more naturalistic stimulus class than pure tones
span.quote: We chose artificial vowels as a more “naturalistic” class of stimuli than pure tones.

span.label: animals allowed to continue testing to satiation and given ad libitum water afterwards
span.quote: To ensure that the animals did not suffer dehydration as a consequence of water restriction, they were allowed to continue the behavioral testing to satiation

span.label: two distinct senses of hippocampal sound response are proposed: a short-latency onset response, present even in sleep and not sound-specific, versus a longer sound-specific response that needs task engagement
span.quote: Based on the current findings and the results of previous experiments we described the existence of two types of hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds: sound-onset responses with very short latency and longer-lasting sound-specific responses that are likely to be present when the animal is actively engaged in the task.

span.label: sound-responsive is defined by ANY of four a-priori bin sizes surviving FDR correction - a disjunctive criterion, so the label mixes fast transient and slow sustained responses
span.quote: A neuron was considered a “sound or reward-encoding” neuron if any of the time bins showed a corrected p -value smaller than 0.05.

span.label: passive here means a different room, different floor, different light and different smell - the novelty of the context is part of the manipulation, not a nuisance
span.quote: Outside the context of the behavioral task, passive exposures to the awake rat were done in an unfamiliar dark plastic bin (33 × 22 × 35 cm) which differed from the training environment by geometry, texture of the floor and the walls, the lighting, and the smell.

span.label: the earlier null from this group's own work is reinterpreted as an artefact of overtraining rather than as an absence of the phenomenon
span.quote: However, in those experiments hippocampal neurons did not respond to sounds when played to the animal not engaged in a discrimination task. These recordings were performed in highly over trained animals and it is possible that some of the features of neuronal responses were absent due to repetition of the same stimuli over many thousands of trials.

span.label: contradicts → Itskov et al. (2012), which found no hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds outside the categorization task
span.quote: The absence of neuronal responses to sound stimuli outside the categorization task (Itskov et al., 2012 ) seems at the first glance inconsistent with the results of our current experiment, where we have found that hippocampal neurons responded to the sound stimuli presented during passive wakefulness.

span.label: builds-on → Brankack and Buzsaki (1986) on short-latency hippocampal responses to sounds
span.quote: Short latency responses to sounds in hippocampus have previously described in the literature (Brankack and Buzsaki, 1986 ).

span.label: extends → Rudoy et al. (2009) sustained EEG response to auditory cues presented to sleeping humans
span.quote: The latter finding might be related to the sustained EEG response found in Rudoy et al. ( 2009 ) after presentation of auditory stimuli to humans during sleep.

span.label: qualifies → the same group's earlier finding that hippocampal neurons do not respond to sounds outside a discrimination task
span.quote: However, in those experiments hippocampal neurons did not respond to sounds when played to the animal not engaged in a discrimination task. These recordings were performed in highly over trained animals and it is possible that some of the features of neuronal responses were absent due to repetition of the same stimuli over many thousands of trials.

span.label: supports → reports that hippocampal neurons represent non-spatial variables including sounds, textures, odours and taste
span.quote: To investigate how hippocampal neurons code behaviorally salient stimuli, we recorded from neurons in the CA1 region of hippocampus in rats while they learned to associate the presence of sound with water reward.

span.label: supports → the established spatial selectivity of hippocampal neurons, reproduced here as location coding at the two ports
span.quote: Forty-one percent of tested neurons (24 out of 58) discriminated between right and left nosepokes (see Figure 3A ; p < 0.05, corrected, rank sum test on firing rates 400 ms before the nose pokes, see Materials and Methods).

span.label: onset response —distinct-from→ sound-specific
span.note: the paper's central proposal: two response types separated by latency, duration and whether task engagement is required
span.quote: Based on the current findings and the results of previous experiments we described the existence of two types of hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds: sound-onset responses with very short latency and longer-lasting sound-specific responses that are likely to be present when the animal is actively engaged in the task.

span.label: sound-specific —distinct-from→ passive listening
span.note: none of the passively responding neurons distinguished between sounds
span.quote: None of the three sound-responding neurons discriminated between different sounds i.e., their responses to different sounds were identical.

span.label: hippocampus —operationalised-as→ place
span.note: location coding is reproduced here as discrimination between the two nose pokes
span.quote: Forty-one percent of tested neurons (24 out of 58) discriminated between right and left nosepokes (see Figure 3A ; p < 0.05, corrected, rank sum test on firing rates 400 ms before the nose pokes, see Materials and Methods).

span.label: adaptation —causes→ onset response
span.note: weak and preventive: the design guards against adaptation rather than demonstrating it
span.quote: The long inter-stimulus interval was intended to reduce the animal's adaptation to stimulus repetitions

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
span.quote: Firing rates in each time bin were compared using Wilcoxon rank-sum test for two independent samples (Siegel and Castellan, 1988 ).

span.label: false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons
span.term: false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons
span.quote: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate corrections were used to correct for multiple comparisons (FDR, Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995 ).

span.label: sign test
span.quote: Firing rate values in each of them were compared to firing rate values in 50 ms baseline (sign test for dependent measurements, Siegel and Castellan, 1988 ).

span.label: paired t-test
span.quote: The average time of waiting in no-sound-no-reward trials was 5.09 ± 0.19 s (SEM). Waiting time decreased over the course of the session ( p < 0.001, paired-sample t -test).

span.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
span.quote: We found only one neuron with significant sound identity-dependent responses ( p = 0.0101, Kruskal–Wallis test) comparing responses to three sounds, two artificial vowels and the novel noise-like sound.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: The average time of waiting in no-sound-no-reward trials was 5.09 ± 0.19 s (SEM). Waiting time decreased over the course of the session ( p < 0.001, paired-sample t -test).

span.label: median and interquartile range (box plot)
span.quote: On each box, the central mark is the median, the edges of the box are the 25th and 75th percentiles, the whiskers extend to the most extreme data points not considering outliers; outliers are plotted individually as dots.

span.label: cluster analysis (automatic spike sorting)
span.quote: Spikes were presorted automatically using KlustaKwik (Harris et al., 2000 ), using waveform energy on each of the four channels of the tetrode as coordinates in a 4 dimensional feature space.

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test in 50 ms bins
span.term: Wilcoxon rank-sum test in 50 ms bins
span.quote: Forty-one percent of tested neurons (24 out of 58) discriminated between right and left nosepokes (see Figure 3A ; p < 0.05, corrected, rank sum test on firing rates 400 ms before the nose pokes, see Materials and Methods).

span.label: Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate
span.quote: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate corrections were used to correct for multiple comparisons

span.label: four a-priori bin sizes with a disjunctive criterion
span.term: four a-priori bin sizes with a disjunctive criterion
span.quote: To take into account the variability of the responses (e.g., fast transient or sustained responses), we used four a-priori defined bin sizes (50 ms, 500 ms, 1 and 2 s).

span.label: Forty-one percent of the neurons recorded during the task (24 of 58) fired differently at the right versus the left nosepoke, confirming strong spatial selectivity in this paradigm.
span.quote: Forty-one percent of tested neurons (24 out of 58) discriminated between right and left nosepokes

span.label: Eleven of 58 task-recorded cells (19%) responded within the first 300 ms after sound onset, and 14 (24%) responded at reward delivery.
span.quote: Out of 58 cells recorded in the task, 11 cells responded in the first 300 ms upon sound presentation

span.label: Sound-responsive and reward-responsive populations were completely non-overlapping: no single cell responded to both events.
span.quote: There were no cells with responses to both sound and reward.

span.label: During passive listening in a novel box outside the task, 3 of 25 recorded hippocampal neurons were sound-sensitive, two increasing and one decreasing their firing rate.
span.quote: Three out of 25 neurons recorded during the awake passive conditions were classified as sound-sensitive

span.label: During sleep, 8 of 33 recorded neurons (24%) showed significant sound-evoked responses, five with decreased and three with increased firing rate.
span.quote: Twenty-four percent of recorded neurons (8 out of 33) exhibited significant sound-evoked responses.

span.label: Response latencies during sleep fell between 50 and 150 ms after sound onset.
span.quote: Across neurons, latency ranged from 50 to 150 ms.

span.label: Long-lasting sustained responses occurred only during sleep, and sleep responses were on average roughly twice as long as responses during passive wakefulness.
span.quote: Long lasting responses to sounds were unique to responses recorded during sleep (Figure 6 ).

span.label: Almost no neuron distinguished which sound was played: only one cell showed sound-identity-dependent responses across the two vowels and the novel noise.
span.quote: We found only one neuron with significant sound identity-dependent responses ( p = 0.0101, Kruskal–Wallis test) comparing responses to three sounds, two artificial vowels and the novel noise-like sound.

span.label: Rats waited about 5.09 s at the nosepoke on unrewarded trials, and this waiting time shrank across the session, indicating the sound had become a reward cue and its absence a signal to switch ports.
span.quote: Importantly, in the “unlucky” trials the animals decreased waiting time over the course of the session, suggesting that the occurrence of the sound became associated with the water reward and absence of sound became a cue to go to the alternate nose poke (see Results).

span.label: Hippocampal neurons respond to passively presented sounds in both quiet wakefulness and sleep, contradicting the authors' own earlier null result in over-trained animals.
span.quote: In this study we show that a significant subset of hippocampal neurons responds to sounds presented passively to a rat during both quiet wakefulness and during sleep.

span.label: 41% of neurons, 24 of 58, discriminated between the two nose pokes
span.quote: Forty-one percent of tested neurons (24 out of 58) discriminated between right and left nosepokes (see Figure 3A ; p < 0.05, corrected, rank sum test on firing rates 400 ms before the nose pokes, see Materials and Methods).

span.label: 11 of 58 cells responded within 300 ms of sound onset and 14 responded at reward, with no overlap between the two sets
span.quote: Out of 58 cells recorded in the task, 11 cells responded in the first 300 ms upon sound presentation (19%, p < 0.05, rank sum tests done in 50 ms windows, corrected for testing six time points and also four different bin sizes, see Materials and Methods). Fourteen (24%) responded upon the reward delivery (Figure 3B ). There were no cells with responses to both sound and reward.

span.label: three of 25 neurons responded to sounds during passive wakefulness, two increasing and one decreasing
span.quote: Three out of 25 neurons recorded during the awake passive conditions were classified as sound-sensitive (see Materials and Methods, p -values were 0.0029, 0.0000016, and 0.01, corrected).

span.label: eight of 33 neurons responded during sleep, five decreasing and three increasing
span.quote: Twenty-four percent of recorded neurons (8 out of 33) exhibited significant sound-evoked responses. Across neurons, latency ranged from 50 to 150 ms. In five cases firing rate decreased after sound presentation, in three cases the firing rate increased.

span.label: long-lasting responses over 1 s were unique to sleep, and sleep responses began slightly earlier
span.quote: Long lasting responses to sounds were unique to responses recorded during sleep (Figure 6 ). The responses to sounds during sleep were on average almost twice as long as the response to sounds presented during passive wakefulness (Figure 6F ). Responses to sounds during sleep also appeared slightly earlier than the responses during passive wakefulness (Figure 6E ).

span.label: none of the passively responsive neurons distinguished between the sounds
span.quote: None of the three sound-responding neurons discriminated between different sounds i.e., their responses to different sounds were identical.

span.label: waiting time on unrewarded trials fell across the session, showing the animals learned the sound-reward contingency
span.quote: The average time of waiting in no-sound-no-reward trials was 5.09 ± 0.19 s (SEM). Waiting time decreased over the course of the session ( p < 0.001, paired-sample t -test).

span.label: "location-encoding" neuron
span.quote: A neuron was considered to distinguish between the two nose pokes and therefore to be a “location-encoding” neuron if any of the time bins showed a corrected p -value smaller than 0.05.

span.label: sound-responsive neuron
span.quote: A neuron was considered sound-responsive if any of the time bins showed a corrected p -value smaller than 0.05.

span.label: latency of the response
span.quote: Latency of the responses was calculated as time of the first bin after sound onset with activity significantly different from baseline.

span.label: "lottery" task
span.quote: During the recording sessions (referred to as “lottery,” see below) the sounds were presented with 50% probability for a given nose poke entry.

span.label: two types of hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds
span.term: two types of hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds
span.quote: Based on the current findings and the results of previous experiments we described the existence of two types of hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds: sound-onset responses with very short latency and longer-lasting sound-specific responses that are likely to be present when the animal is actively engaged in the task.

span.label: sound or reward-encoding neuron, by any surviving bin
span.term: sound or reward-encoding neuron, by any surviving bin
span.quote: A neuron was considered a “sound or reward-encoding” neuron if any of the time bins showed a corrected p -value smaller than 0.05.

span.label: the two response types
span.quote: Based on the current findings and the results of previous experiments we described the existence of two types of hippocampal neuronal responses to sounds: sound-onset responses with very short latency and longer-lasting sound-specific responses that are likely to be present when the animal is actively engaged in the task.

span.label: sound presence on a trial ("lucky" vs "unlucky"), assigned at random
span.term: sound presence on a trial ("lucky" vs "unlucky"), assigned at random
span.quote: Whether the current trial would turn out to be “lucky” or “unlucky” was determined randomly by software.

span.label: behavioural state / context in which the sounds were delivered (task, passive wakefulness, sleep)
span.term: behavioural state / context in which the sounds were delivered (task, passive wakefulness, sleep)
span.quote: This study set out to test how neurons in rat hippocampus represent auditory stimuli in the context of a behavioral task, during passive exposure and during sleep.

span.label: sound identity (two familiar reward-associated vowels vs a novel noise-like sound), presented pseudo-randomly
span.term: sound identity (two familiar reward-associated vowels vs a novel noise-like sound), presented pseudo-randomly
span.quote: Three types of sound stimuli (familiar vowel associated with the right well, familiar vowel associated with a left well, and a novel noise-like sound) were presented pseudo-randomly, so that no sound was repeated more than two times in a row.

span.label: firing rate of CA1 neurons in successive time bins
span.term: firing rate of CA1 neurons in successive time bins
span.quote: Wilcoxon rank-sum test for two independent samples was used to compare the firing rates, bin by bin, in “lucky” trials versus not reward trials.

span.label: time the rat waited in the nosepoke
span.term: time the rat waited in the nosepoke
span.quote: The average time of waiting in no-sound-no-reward trials was 5.09 ± 0.19 s (SEM). Waiting time decreased over the course of the session ( p < 0.001, paired-sample t -test).

span.label: animal's spatial position and motivational state, held identical across sound and no-sound trials
span.term: animal's spatial position and motivational state, held identical across sound and no-sound trials
span.quote: Trials with and without sound presentation were compared, assuring that the animal was in exactly the same position and motivational state in both types of trials.

span.label: inter-stimulus interval kept long (25-30 s) to hold adaptation to repeated stimuli down
span.term: inter-stimulus interval kept long (25-30 s) to hold adaptation to repeated stimuli down
span.quote: The long inter-stimulus interval was intended to reduce the animal's adaptation to stimulus repetitions (Ulanovsky et al., 2004 ).

span.label: presence or absence of sound on a trial
span.term: presence or absence of sound on a trial
span.quote: Trials with and without sound presentation were compared, assuring that the animal was in exactly the same position and motivational state in both types of trials.

span.label: which nose poke the animal is visiting
span.term: which nose poke the animal is visiting
span.quote: Forty-one percent of tested neurons (24 out of 58) discriminated between right and left nosepokes (see Figure 3A ; p < 0.05, corrected, rank sum test on firing rates 400 ms before the nose pokes, see Materials and Methods).

span.label: behavioural state: task, passive wakefulness, sleep
span.term: behavioural state: task, passive wakefulness, sleep
span.quote: In the current experiment we characterized responses of hippocampal neurons to behaviorally relevant sounds which were played during sleep and to awake passively listening rats. In the behavioral task, the sounds cued the upcoming release of a reward. Outside the task, the sounds were unrelated to the animal's behavior.

span.label: 24 out of 58 — neurons that discriminated between the right and left nosepoke (41% of tested neurons)
span.quote: Forty-one percent of tested neurons (24 out of 58) discriminated between right and left nosepokes

span.label: 24% — proportion of neurons recorded during sleep (8 of 33) with significant sound-evoked responses
span.quote: Twenty-four percent of recorded neurons (8 out of 33) exhibited significant sound-evoked responses.

span.label: 14 (24%) — task-recorded cells that responded at the moment of water reward delivery
span.quote: Fourteen (24%) responded upon the reward delivery (Figure 3B ).

span.label: 5.09 ± 0.19 s — mean (± SEM) time the rats waited in the nosepoke on trials with no sound and no reward
span.quote: The average time of waiting in no-sound-no-reward trials was 5.09 ± 0.19 s (SEM). Waiting time decreased over the course of the session ( p < 0.001, paired-sample t -test).

span.label: 50 to 150 ms — range of sound-response latencies across neurons recorded during sleep
span.quote: Across neurons, latency ranged from 50 to 150 ms.

span.label: 1–2 s — duration of the long-lasting sound responses observed during sleep
span.quote: During sleep the short-latency responses in hippocampus are intermingled with long lasting responses which in the current experiment could last for 1–2 s.

span.label: 0.2 ms — spike width (measured at 25% of spike amplitude) of the two example sleep-responsive neurons, suggesting putative interneurons
span.quote: Both neurons depicted on this figure had narrow spikes (Figures 5E and J ), 0.2 ms when measured on 25% of spike amplitude.

span.label: two animals — number of implanted rats (out of six trained, four implanted) that yielded neuronal data suitable for analysis
span.quote: Neuronal data suitable for analysis was collected from two animals.

span.label: 8% during passive wakefulness and 25% during sleep, as stated in the ABSTRACT — the abstract's summary percentages - see the results rows below, which do not reconstruct the 8% without assuming a narrower denominator
span.quote: When the sounds were played during passive wakefulness, 8% of neurons responded with short latency onset responses; 25% of neurons responded to sounds when they were played during sleep.

span.label: three out of 25 neurons, which is 12% — the passive-wakefulness result as given in the RESULTS section
span.quote: Three out of 25 neurons recorded during the awake passive conditions were classified as sound-sensitive (see Materials and Methods, p -values were 0.0029, 0.0000016, and 0.01, corrected).

span.label: two increased and one decreased — the direction split among those three - counting only the increases would give 2 of 25, which IS 8%
span.quote: Two of the neurons showed a significantly increased firing rate in response to the sound, and one a decreased the firing rate.

span.label: 24%, eight out of 33 — the sleep result in the RESULTS section, against 25% in the abstract
span.quote: Twenty-four percent of recorded neurons (8 out of 33) exhibited significant sound-evoked responses. Across neurons, latency ranged from 50 to 150 ms. In five cases firing rate decreased after sound presentation, in three cases the firing rate increased.

span.label: six trained, four implanted, two yielding usable data — the animal attrition
span.quote: Out of the six animals trained to perform the behavioral task, four were implanted using microdrives for chronic recordings. Neuronal data suitable for analysis was collected from two animals.

span.label: 5.09 plus or minus 0.19 s — average waiting time on no-sound trials
span.quote: The average time of waiting in no-sound-no-reward trials was 5.09 ± 0.19 s (SEM). Waiting time decreased over the course of the session ( p < 0.001, paired-sample t -test).
